records.title: Additional information
records.content: This page gathers what does not fit under Guides or Reference: licensing of the default stack, how to reach the people behind a Nebula deployment, where release notes and the changelog will be published, and where the FAQ lives.

records.title: Additional information
records.content: Every component that runs by default in the checked-in Compose stack is open source, with one source-available exception that is disclosed rather than hidden (the bundled but inactive Terraform binary is a second, opt-in exception). Identity has no licensing footprint at all: Nebula speaks standard OpenID Connect and trusts any spec-faithful issuer, so a fully open-source deployment can pair it with Keycloak (Apache-2.0, CNCF Incubating) while an enterprise can point it at Entra ID, Auth0, or Okta without changing a line of code. Component Role Licence Notes Nebula (core, sidecars, SPA, contracts) The platform Apache-2.0 REUSE-compliant SPDX headers OpenTofu 1.12.6 Default IaC engine in the iac sidecar MPL-2.0 (Linux Foundation) Digest-pinned. The same image also bundles HashiCorp Terraform 1.16.0 (BUSL-1.1, not OSI), downloaded and checksum-verified at build time and selectable via IAC_BINARY=terraform; running it makes your use subject to its licence terms RustFS Default, bundled S3-compatible object storage for artifacts (and for Terraform state where that is enabled) Apache-2.0 Rust implementation of the S3 API; AWS S3 or Azure Blob Storage selectable via storage.provider, or any other S3-compatible endpoint via the RUSTFS provider PostgreSQL 17 core-db and phoenix-db PostgreSQL Licence — Redis 8 Fail-open cache Tri-licensed: AGPLv3 (OSI) / RSALv2 / SSPLv1 AGPLv3 option restored in Redis 8.0 nginx Reverse proxy and SPA host BSD-2-Clause — FastAPI, LiteLLM, React, oidc-client-ts Framework, model router, portal, OIDC client MIT — OpenTelemetry / OpenInference Tracing standard and semantic conventions Apache-2.0 OpenTelemetry is CNCF Graduated (2026-05-21) Arize Phoenix Trace UI and runtime prompt registry Elastic License 2.0 (source-available, not OSI-approved) The only non-OSI component; disclosed in all public material OpenID Connect Authentication protocol Open standard (OpenID Foundation) No component shipped; any compliant IdP

records.title: Additional information
records.content: Three channels, each with its own purpose: Support request in the web application — questions about your own Nebula deployment or about one of your sessions. It reaches the reviewers in your deployment, not the Nebula project. Issue tracker — bugs and feature requests in Nebula itself. Check the existing issues first; Contributing covers what happens next. Disclosure submission program — security vulnerabilities, reported privately and never through a public GitHub issue.

records.title: Additional information
records.content: Any signed-in user can send a support request from inside the web application. It goes to the people who hold the reviewer roles in your own Nebula deployment — colleagues on your platform team, not the Nebula project — through the channel your platform team connected (Slack in the reference setup), with a copy addressed to you. From the browser, the chat-bubble Support icon in the header opens a form for up to 500 characters, plain text only — HTML and code formatting are rejected. The message carries your e-mail, the session id, the repository, branch, request, status, and a link to the session automatically, so you do not need to copy those in yourself. Contact Team (on a locked session) and Request Review (on the apply confirmation) send the same kind of message, pre-filled for that session, and flagged as a warning when the plan deletes or recreates resources. "Your question has been sent successfully" confirms delivery; "Your question could not be sent. Notifications are disabled." means your deployment has not connected a notification channel — use your organization’s usual support route and quote the session id. The form calls POST /api/v1/notifications. The core forwards the request to the notifications sidecar with an audience made of the caller’s e-mail plus every user holding a panel role of editor or higher, and the bundled sidecar posts it to Slack. When services.notifications.enabled is false the route answers 503 Notifications are disabled.; when delivery fails it answers 502 Notification was not delivered.

records.title: Additional information
records.content: Report a security vulnerability through the disclosure submission program, in English — never through a public GitHub issue. The security team acknowledges a report within 48 hours, investigates its severity, and develops, tests, and publishes a fix and an advisory. See the security policy for the full process and the safe-harbor terms covering researchers who report in good faith.

records.title: Additional information
records.content: Nebula has not published a tagged release yet. When it does, the curated highlights of each release — what is new and what it changes for the people using it — will be listed here and on the project’s GitHub Releases page.

records.title: Additional information
records.content: The unabridged, commit-level record of changes is the repository’s commit history; it is not duplicated here. Once releases exist, each GitHub Release carries the complete list of additions, changes, fixes, and deprecations since the previous one.

records.title: About Nebula
records.content: Nebula is an LLM-powered platform that turns natural-language requests into compliant, Terraform-compatible infrastructure-as-code (IaC). Platform engineers and application developers describe the infrastructure they need, and Nebula’s agents generate the corresponding code, guided by the organization’s own standards. It runs as a layered FastAPI orchestration core alongside four contract-first FastAPI sidecars — the IaC engine, repository mapping, notifications, and authorization — behind an nginx edge that also serves a React single-page application and proxies the API. Every state change and every blocking decision — the in-flight guard, validation, the compliance verdict, the session lock, apply — is computed by application code, not by a model, and applying a reviewed plan is always a human action.

records.title: About Nebula
records.content: Pan, zoom, search, trace a relationship, switch themes. Open in a new tab /* Progressive enhancement for the block above. Guarded so that a page holding several diagrams runs this once, and deferred to DOMContentLoaded because a parse-time script cannot yet see the diagrams below it. */ (function () { if (window.__archifyEmbed) return window.__archifyEmbed = true /* The viewer's own interactive chrome. Its toolbar and zoom bar are position:fixed, so they always reach the bottom of whatever viewport the iframe gives them -- measuring them would make the height measurement below a fixpoint that can never shrink. Same selector list as docs/diagrams/capture-png.mjs, which hides them instead; here they stay visible and are only excluded from the measurement. */ var CHROME = '.toolbar, .diagram-nav, .focus-chip, .guided-views, .archify-toast, .no-print' var style = document.createElement('style') style.textContent = [ '.archify-actions{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:.35rem .9rem;align-items:baseline;', 'margin-block:-.65rem 1.5rem;font-size:.875rem;line-height:1.5}', '.archify-hint{opacity:.72}', '.archify-frame{width:100%;border:0;display:block}', /* A viewer is ~800KB and takes real time to arrive, so it loads out of the way while the still stays on screen, and is only swapped in once it has something to show. Off-screen rather than display:none: a display:none iframe has no viewport, so the application inside would not lay out, and revealing it would show an empty frame anyway -- which is the whole failure this avoids. */ '.archify-frame[data-archify-loading]{position:absolute;left:-99999px;top:0}', /* Only while the viewer is live. The still image is centred by the theme inside the narrower .imageblock; the frame is centred by this margin inside the wider one. */ '.imageblock.archify-live{margin-inline:auto}', /* The theme insets an image block's contents by 40px, which puts the diagram 40px right of every heading and paragraph on the page. Those do line up with each other: a heading's box starts 64px further left than its text, because the theme carves that gutter with a negative margin and an equal padding to hold the hover anchor. So the column edge is where the text sits, and the diagram was the one thing off it. Dropped on both forms, so activating a block does not shift it. */ '.imageblock.archify-block > .content{padding-inline:0}', ].join('') document.head.appendChild(style) /* The .imageblock wrapper is what escapes the 820px .sectionbody cap (`width: min(calc(var(--content-max-width)*1.25), var(--doc-inset-cap))`), so the viewer is swapped in inside it rather than in place of it. */ function blockFor (actions) { var el = actions.previousElementSibling while (el && !el.classList.contains('imageblock')) el = el.previousElementSibling return el } /* Width is the only lever on how large the viewer draws: its SVG comes out at roughly 0.9x the viewport width it is given, and viewport height barely moves it. But --doc-inset-cap holds .imageblock at 1025px however wide the window gets, which on a large display leaves the whole right half of the article column unused. Track the column instead, so a 2560px screen gets a 1490px frame rather than the still's 945px. */ function columnWidth (block) { var column = block.closest('.doc') return column ? column.clientWidth : 0 } function widen (block) { var width = columnWidth(block) if (width) block.style.width = width + 'px' } /* Height of the real content, which is not the same as the document height: the viewer is a full-viewport application, so both scrollHeight and body height just echo back the height we set. Measure the lowest visible content edge instead, ignoring the fixed chrome. */ function contentHeight (frame) { var doc = frame.contentDocument if (!doc) return 0 var view = doc.defaultView var root = doc.querySelector('.container') || doc.body var nodes = root.querySelectorAll('*') var bottom = 0 for (var i = 0; i < nodes.length; i++) { var node = nodes[i] var computed = view.getComputedStyle(node) if (computed.display === 'none' || computed.visibility === 'hidden' || computed.opacity === '0') continue if (computed.position === 'fixed' || node.closest(CHROME)) continue var rect = node.getBoundingClientRect() if (!rect.width || !rect.height) continue bottom = Math.max(bottom, rect.bottom) } return bottom ? Math.ceil(bottom + 24) : 0 } /* A wider frame makes the viewer draw a larger diagram, which makes it taller, which is the measurement that sized the frame. Settle it over a few bounded passes instead of assuming one is enough, and stop once the change is not worth another reflow. A measurement of zero means the viewer has not laid itself out yet, not that it never will: each one is a whole application, and end-to-end-flow loads five of them at once over a cold cache. Keep waiting, because giving up here strands the frame at its seeded height for good. */ function fit (frame, pass, waits) { var height = contentHeight(frame) if (!height) { if ((waits || 0) < 60) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, pass, (waits || 0) + 1) }, 250) return } var current = parseInt(frame.style.height, 10) || 0 if (Math.abs(height - current) < 8) return frame.style.height = height + 'px' if ((pass || 0) < 3) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, (pass || 0) + 1, 0) }, 250) } /* Replaces one still with its viewer, then calls `done` to free the slot for the next one -- on load, or on the breaker below, whichever comes first. The still stays on screen for the whole download. An earlier version put the frame in place the moment it was created, which left a blank grey panel where the diagram had been until ~800KB arrived: on a fast static server that is a flicker, on anything slower it is the whole reading experience. So the frame loads off-screen, at the size it is about to occupy, and the swap happens in one synchronous block. */ function activate (actions, done) { var block = blockFor(actions) if (!block || block.classList.contains('archify-live')) return done() var content = block.firstElementChild || block var still = content.querySelector('img') var frame = document.createElement('iframe') frame.className = 'archify-frame' frame.title = actions.dataset.archifyTitle || 'Interactive diagram' /* Load it at the size it will be revealed at, so the viewer lays out for the real column and appearing costs no second reflow. Antora writes no width/height on the still, so one that has not decoded yet measures zero: fall back to a nominal height rather than a collapsed frame. */ var seed = still ? Math.round(still.getBoundingClientRect().height) : 0 frame.style.height = (seed > 120 ? seed : 620) + 'px' frame.style.width = (columnWidth(block) || block.clientWidth || 900) + 'px' frame.setAttribute('data-archify-loading', '') /* Everything that makes the frame visible, in one go, so no intermediate state is ever painted. The frame is never moved in the DOM -- re-inserting an iframe reloads it, which would throw away the wait -- so the still is removed around it instead. */ function reveal () { frame.removeAttribute('data-archify-loading') frame.style.width = '' /* .imageblock is display:flex and .content is a shrink-wrapping flex item: the image sized it by its own intrinsic width, but an iframe has none, so .content would collapse to the UA's 300px iframe default and the frame's width:100% would resolve against an indefinite container. Pin .content to the flex container's width so the percentage has something definite to resolve against. */ content.style.width = '100%' block.classList.add('archify-live') widen(block) for (var i = content.children.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (content.children[i] !== frame) content.children[i].remove() } } /* One viewer loads at a time, so a frame that never fires load would hold the queue for good and strand every diagram below it as a still. Release the slot after a generous wait; this frame still reveals itself if it turns up late. */ var settled = false function settle () { if (settled) return settled = true done() } setTimeout(settle, 15000) frame.addEventListener('load', function () { /* The viewer repeats its own title as an <h1> above the diagram, and every page that embeds one already carries that line as the section heading right above the frame. Two of the same sentence is one too many, and at column width the repeat wraps onto a second line and runs into the viewer's own toolbar. Hidden here rather than removed from the specification: a title is required there, and the "Open in a new tab" page has no surrounding heading to make it redundant. Same document, same origin, so this is a stylesheet and not a message. */ var inner = frame.contentDocument if (inner) { var hide = inner.createElement('style') hide.textContent = '.container > .header{display:none}' inner.head.appendChild(hide) } /* `load` means the viewer's assets arrived and its scripts ran, not that it has drawn: the SVG appears in a later layout pass. Revealing on load alone shows the viewer's own empty panel for a frame or two, so wait for the drawing to exist -- briefly, and then reveal anyway, because a viewer that never draws must not keep the still forever. */ var tries = 0 ;(function ready () { var drawn = false try { drawn = !!(inner && inner.querySelector('svg')) } catch (e) { drawn = true } if (!drawn && ++tries <= 20) return void setTimeout(ready, 100) reveal() settle() /* Only now is the frame in the flow at its final width, so this is where the height measurement belongs. */ setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, 0) }, 400) var width = 0 new ResizeObserver(function () { /* Width only: observing our own height would loop against fit(). */ var next = Math.round(frame.getBoundingClientRect().width) if (next === width) return width = next fit(frame, 0) }).observe(frame) })() }) content.appendChild(frame) frame.src = actions.dataset.archifySrc } /* A page can hold five of these and each is a whole application of roughly 800KB, so they are loaded strictly one at a time. Serial, not merely staggered. An earlier version started one every 900ms, which on a slow origin simply put all five in flight together: a browser opens about six connections per origin, five long downloads take nearly all of them, and the next click on the navigation sidebar gets no socket at all. That is not a slow page, it is a page that has stopped answering -- the network panel shows the navigation cancelled with zero bytes transferred. One viewer at a time bounds the cost to a single connection however slow the origin is, and the reader keeps a still until its replacement is ready, so nothing is lost by waiting. Proximity decides the order and never whether. Two earlier versions let it decide whether, and both stranded the lower diagrams as stills for good: the reader saw a tiny illegible image where a viewer should be. The cause outlives either mechanism. Antora writes no width or height on a still, so every image reflows everything below it as it decodes -- which means a block can be carried into range with no event to announce it. An IntersectionObserver's one-shot entry arrives against a position the block no longer holds; a rect read on scroll is never stale, but nothing reads it once the reader stops scrolling. Working through the whole queue removes that class of failure instead of widening the window it hides in: being near a diagram only brings it forward. */ function enhance () { var pending = [] var actions = document.querySelectorAll('.archify-actions[data-archify-src]') for (var i = 0; i < actions.length; i++) { var block = blockFor(actions[i]) if (!block) continue /* Marks the blocks this script owns, so the stylesheet above can reach them while they are still stills. */ block.classList.add('archify-block') pending.push(actions[i]) } if (!pending.length) return var queued = false var running = false function stop () { window.removeEventListener('scroll', schedule) window.removeEventListener('resize', schedule) } /* Leaving the page ends the queue. Without this, a click on the navigation sidebar races a pump that is about to start another ~800KB viewer: the browser asks for the next document while this page opens one more connection for a viewer nobody will ever see, and on a slow origin the navigation is what waits. The reader reads that as a page that has stopped answering. Nothing below needs the queue once the document is on its way out. */ window.addEventListener('pagehide', function () { pending.length = 0 stop() }) /* One observer for the whole column, not one per diagram. Every live block tracks the same element, so five separate observers on it did the same work five times over on every resize. */ var column = document.querySelector('.doc') if (column) { new ResizeObserver(function () { var live = document.querySelectorAll('.imageblock.archify-live') for (var i = 0; i < live.length; i++) widen(live[i]) }).observe(column) } /* The one place a viewer is ever started. Nothing else calls activate, so there is exactly one download in flight no matter what triggers a pump -- scroll, resize, or the previous one finishing. */ function pump () { if (running || !pending.length) return running = true activate(pending.shift(), function () { running = false if (pending.length) setTimeout(pump, 250) else stop() }) } /* Reorders what is left so anything the reader can nearly see goes next, and never activates anything itself. A diagram already passed keeps its place in the queue: the saving worth having is not loading five viewers at once, not reclaiming one that has scrolled off the top. */ function promote () { queued = false var visible = [] var rest = [] for (var i = 0; i < pending.length; i++) { var block = blockFor(pending[i]) var close = block && block.getBoundingClientRect().top <= window.innerHeight + 400 ;(close ? visible : rest).push(pending[i]) } pending = visible.concat(rest) pump() } function schedule () { if (queued) return queued = true requestAnimationFrame(promote) } window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true }) window.addEventListener('resize', schedule) promote() } if (document.readyState === 'loading') document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', enhance) else enhance() })() The core platform components — the core orchestration API, the proxy (nginx), core-db (PostgreSQL), redis, object-storage, and the phoenix observability stack — run as shipped and are configured through config.yaml and the .env files. You never reimplement them; in production you replace only the bundled datastores. Four sidecars are the integration points between Nebula and your organization: iac (executes the IaC engine; mandatory, always on), notifications (posts session outcomes to Slack; disabled by default), mapping (resolves a repository reference; disabled by default), and authz (applies cloud-project authorization policy; disabled by default). Each implements an OpenAPI contract, so any implementation of that contract can replace the bundled reference. A disabled sidecar is never contacted. The React single-page application is the user-facing portal, served by the proxy. The whole stack runs from one Docker Compose stack, with nginx as the only public entry point.

records.title: About Nebula
records.content: Layered orchestration core — sessions run through filtering, generation, validation, and reporting phases, computed by application code, see Architecture. Four replaceable sidecars — the IaC engine, repository mapping, notifications, and authorization each implement an OpenAPI contract, so an organization can swap in its own implementation. Human-gated apply — every blocking decision is computed by code, and applying a reviewed plan is always an explicit human action. OpenTofu by default — the bundled iac sidecar runs OpenTofu, with HashiCorp Terraform also bundled and selectable via IAC_BINARY. Nebula’s runtime components, internal layering, and end-to-end request flow are covered in Architecture. To run the bundled stack locally, see Quickstart. From there, Guides walks through each task the web application supports, and Reference holds the configuration, environment-variable, role, and API details those guides point at.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: Short answers for people using the Nebula web application. The longer explanations are in the Make a request guide; mode-by-mode behavior is in Comparing the operating modes. If the answer you need is not here, see Support requests.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: Why are the drift modes and Import Infrastructure greyed out? They require the devops operation role. New users start as developer. Ask your administrator to change your role in the admin portal; it takes effect on your next page load. Can other people see my sessions? Only reviewers who hold a panel role (viewer, editor, or admin) can read them, including the conversation. Nobody but you can continue, merge, or apply your sessions. Why does the login page say my session has expired? Your identity token expired and the application signed you out. Sign in again. Any Nebula session that was running continues on the server; reopen it from the footer or your user page.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: Do I have to specify every parameter? No. Missing parameters never block a creation request. Nebula applies your organization’s naming conventions, resource defaults, and the placement it finds in the workspace, and it states the assumptions it made in the response. My request was declined. Why? The filter explains the reason in the chat. The four causes are: out of scope (not a Terraform-managed change), prohibited by your organization’s forbidden-actions list, an ambiguous target (name the resource), or a missing referent (the thing you refer to does not exist in that repository and path). Can I ask questions instead of requesting changes? Yes. Inventory, improvement, and impact questions are answered in the chat; the round ends without changes and you can continue with a change request in the same session. Can I request several changes at once? You can, but one intent per request produces better results and clearer reports. Use follow-ups for the next step; they run on the same branch. Why was my repository URL rejected? URLs that embed a user name or token are refused; enter the plain HTTPS URL. Azure DevOps users: the portal’s clone URL starts with https://<org>@dev.azure.com/…​; remove the <org>@ part. Only github.com, gitlab.com (no subgroups), and dev.azure.com are supported for pull requests. The repository must also be reachable by Nebula’s service account. Why does Nebula say it found no IaC paths? It only sees files committed on the repository’s default branch, and it offers a directory only when it contains .tf files and no part of its path is modules, examples, example, or .terraform. Commit the Terraform files to the default branch, or move them out of an excluded directory. The rules are in Repository layout. Why is my directory not offered as an IaC path? Either it sits under an excluded directory name, or it is nested under another directory that already qualifies as a root (for example platform/network/ under a platform/ that has a main.tf); in that case pick the parent, Nebula works from there. Why does the scope field not accept my value? It accepts letters, digits, and hyphens only, up to 64 characters, and lower-cases the value. Underscores, dots, and spaces are not accepted.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: How long does a session take? From a couple of minutes for a small change to considerably longer for large roots: generation and up to five validation attempts run first, then a drift check and the report. The progress screen shows what is happening at each moment. Can I close the browser? Yes. The session runs on the server. Reopen it from the Sessions panel in the footer or from View all sessions on your user page. Why can I not continue a failed session? A failed round ends the session for good. Start a new session; if the failure was "Validation loop exceeded.", make the request more specific or split it. Why does nothing happen when I send a second request while one is running? Only one operation runs per session at a time. Wait for the current round to finish; the input is disabled during a run. What is the branch called? Nebula/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS in UTC, created on the first request of the session. Every round pushes to it.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: What do Low, Medium, and High impact mean? With the default criteria: high is destructive actions, restarts, downtime, or critical networking changes; medium is a significant configuration update that changes behavior without guaranteed downtime; low is isolated new resources or non-disruptive updates such as tags. Is the estimated cost accurate? It is an approximation of fixed monthly prices for the resources in the plan, taken from public pricing pages when the report was written. Usage-based and free resources are listed but not included in the total. Use it to compare options, not as a quote. Where are the compliance findings? They are not displayed in the application. The audit’s outcome is visible as the lock; the reviewers who receive the notification see the summary. Ask them for the rule-level detail. Can I download the plan or the report? Not as files. The plan, report, and changed files are shown inline in the results view and in the session details; the code itself is on the session branch in your repository.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: Why is my session locked? The compliance audit found an error-level or critical violation (with the default rules: changes outside the scope of your request, parts of the request left undone, or a standalone deletion), or the impact was rated High in a deployment that locks on high impact. What can I do while locked? Read everything, continue the conversation, and create the pull request so reviewers can see the diff. Merging and applying are refused. How is a lock released? A reviewer with the editor or admin panel role unlocks the session from the admin panel, or a new request in the same session produces a result that passes cleanly. Why is a deletion I explicitly asked for flagged? The default compliance rule treats any standalone deletion as a critical violation regardless of the request; only a recreate of the same resource is allowed. A reviewer can unlock the session after looking at it, and your organization can adapt the rule.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: Do I have to open a pull request? The API allows a direct apply, but the web application does not offer a standalone Apply button. In practice you reach apply either through Approve PR and Apply, which merges the pull request and then applies, or through the Import Infrastructure mode in the header drop-down, which calls the same apply on the current session and is only selectable with the devops role. So as a developer in the web application, the pull request is the route to apply — which is also the recommended one, because it brings your team’s review and CI into the decision. Reviewers asked for changes. What now? Type the changes as a follow-up request in the same session. The new round pushes to the same branch, so the pull request updates. What exactly does Approve PR and Apply do? After you confirm, it merges the pull request into the default branch and executes the plan you reviewed, without re-planning. The apply-results screen shows what happened. The apply failed. Will Nebula retry? No. The session still closes as completed, with an apply report whose status is the model’s reading of the engine output (normally Failed) and a failure notification to your reviewers, which is the signal keyed to the exit code; nothing is rolled back and nothing is re-run. Read the error in the apply results, fix the cause (often cloud permissions or a resource that changed since the plan), and send a new request, which produces a fresh plan to review. Does Import Infrastructure import my existing resources? Not yet. Today it runs the apply of an existing session’s reviewed plan. Importing unmanaged resources is a planned capability. Where does Terraform state live? Not in the repository, and not in the working copy Nebula creates. Out of the box, Nebula keeps state for you, in a bucket dedicated to state with one state file per project (repository + cloud scope + path). Your platform team can instead configure Nebula to leave it in the remote backend your repository’s own Terraform files declare, exactly as it would if you ran the engine yourself. Either way your pull request contains only your infrastructure code — no state file and no backend file — and there is nothing for you to set per session; the details are in Configure state backends. My plan wants to create resources that already exist. Why? The session is planning against empty state. The usual causes are that your platform team turned off Nebula-managed state and your repository declares no remote backend of its own, that the project’s identity changed — the root-module path moved, the repository was renamed, or a different cloud scope was selected — or that your platform team changed the state backend, which Nebula never migrates. Report it with the session id; an operator can check the state location.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: What data leaves Nebula when I make a request? Your request text, the conversation, the repository files the agent reads, the plan, and validation errors are sent to the language model your platform team configured and stored in the tracing system for review. Do not paste secrets into requests or commit them to the repository. Which cloud credentials does Nebula use? The identity your platform team configured for the execution engine, never yours. Your deployment can also plug in an external authorization service that is asked, at the start of each session, whether you may work on that cloud, repository, and IaC path; in the shipped configuration that service is switched off and no such check runs.

records.title: Frequently asked questions
records.content: How do I contact support? Use the chat-bubble Support icon in the header, or Contact Team on a locked session. The message carries your e-mail, the session id, and the session context automatically and reaches the reviewers of your deployment. Support says notifications are disabled. Your deployment has not connected a notification channel. Use your organization’s usual support route and quote the session id from the session details. What should I include when reporting a problem? The session id, the mode, the repository and path, what you asked, and what you expected instead. Reviewers can then open the session’s history, artifacts, and traces. See Support requests for the full detail on what each support channel carries and how it is routed.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: This glossary lists the terms, abbreviations, and phrases used across the Nebula documentation, together with their definitions. Use this terminology for clarity and consistency when discussing Nebula.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: An independent, second LLM agent that checks a generated plan against the organization’s compliance rules after a generate round. Failing findings — and, optionally, a high-impact verdict — lock the session until a panel editor unlocks it or a later generate round passes clean. See Session locks.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: Infrastructure changes made outside Terraform — for example a console edit or a hotfix — that no longer match the code. Nebula can detect drift and generate code that reconciles it. See Remediate drift.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The phase where a small-model agent classifies a request: a change request proceeds, a question is answered in the conversation, and an out-of-scope, prohibited, or ambiguous request is declined with an explanation. See Make a request.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The phase where the main-model agent edits Terraform files through tools to satisfy the request, committing and pushing the result to the session branch. See Follow a session.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The command-line tool — OpenTofu by default, or HashiCorp Terraform — that the iac sidecar runs to initialize, validate, plan, and apply infrastructure code. See Deployment view.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The operating mode chosen in the web application header: Generate Infrastructure, Partial Drift Remediation, Full Drift Remediation, or Import Infrastructure. The drift and import modes require the devops operation role. See Operating modes.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The bundled, verified default IaC engine (MPL-2.0). HashiCorp Terraform (BUSL-1.1) is also bundled and selectable with IAC_BINARY. See Deployment view.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: developer or devops, assigned per user and checked by the API on every IaC route; devops is above developer and is required for drift remediation. See Roles and permissions.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: An optional, hierarchical role — viewer, editor, or admin — that gates the admin panel: viewer reads cross-user sessions, editor also toggles a session lock, and admin also manages users and roles. See Roles and permissions.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The plan file and validated workspace that a successful generate round renames into the session’s pinned directory, replacing any earlier pin, and that POST /api/v1/iac/apply executes without re-planning. Only generate rounds pin — drift rounds never do — and apply consumes and discards it whatever the outcome. See Merge and apply.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: Nebula’s readable summary of the plan: what is created, updated, deleted, or recreated, the potential impact, and an estimated cost. See Follow a session.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The natural-language text a user submits describing the infrastructure change, the drift to reconcile, or the question to ask. Each request within a session opens a round. See Make a request.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: One request-and-response cycle inside a session, with its own statuses, report, plan, code changes, and pull requests. The first API call creates round 1 with status started and the handler immediately opens round 2 for the actual work; the API exposes both a round’s database id and its per-session number, and the web application labels rounds by number. See Follow a session.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: One conversation with Nebula about one repository. A session owns a Git branch named Nebula/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS (UTC) and a directory on the shared volume, and each user request within it opens a round. See Follow a session.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: A flag on the session that blocks apply and pull-request merge. It is set automatically when the compliance audit fails or, where the deployment enables it, when the impact is High, and cleared either by an admin-panel editor or by a later generate round whose audit passes without a high-impact verdict. Some internal material calls this a plan lock. See Session locks.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: An integration point between Nebula and an organization’s systems, implementing an OpenAPI contract. Any implementation of the contract can replace the bundled reference by pointing services.<name>.endpoint in config.yaml at it. See HTTP APIs.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The phase where the iac sidecar runs init, validate, and plan against the shared workspace to check that the generated code is sound and preview its effect. See Follow a session.

records.title: Glossary
records.content: The per-run directory, shared with the iac sidecar, where Nebula clones the repository and the IaC engine runs its commands. Each run gets its own directory under the session’s path; only the pinned plan is per session. See Deployment view.

records.title: Contributing
records.content: Thank you for your interest in contributing to Nebula. Any contribution is valued and appreciated; the guidelines below keep the project collaborative and respectful. For the local development loop — running the stack, the test suites, type checking, and linting — see Development.

records.title: Contributing
records.content: Before contributing code, sign the Contributor License Agreement (CLA). Instructions are at InditexTech/foss. By participating in the project you agree to abide by the rules and principles set out in the code of conduct. Nebula adheres to the general Inditex Tech Code of Conduct; direct any inquiry about it to oso@inditex.com. Check existing issues and pull requests before starting work, to avoid duplication. If you take on an existing issue, comment on it so other contributors know it is in progress. Discuss and gather feedback from the community before making significant changes to the project’s structure or architecture.

records.title: Contributing
records.content: Open an issue to discuss and gather feedback on the feature or fix you wish to address. Security vulnerabilities are the exception: report them through the disclosure submission program as described in the security policy, never through a public issue. Fork the repository and clone it to your local machine. Create a new branch to work on your contribution: git checkout -b your-branch-name. Make the necessary changes in your local branch, following Development to run the stack and its checks. Ensure that your code follows the established project style and formatting guidelines. Perform testing to ensure your changes do not introduce errors. Make clear and descriptive commits that explain your changes. Push your branch to the remote repository: git push origin your-branch-name. Open a pull request describing your changes and linking the corresponding issue. Await comments and discussions on your pull request. Make any necessary modifications based on the feedback you receive. Once your pull request is approved, your contribution is merged into the main branch.

records.title: Contributing
records.content: Fill in the pull-request template (.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md) and link the issue it addresses. Include UI screenshots for visible changes. Document any new changes or features you add, so other contributors and users understand your work and its purpose. Keep the commit history clean and organized: divide your changes into logical, descriptive commits. Commit subjects must follow the Conventional Commits Specification (for example fix(core): release session lock); CI rejects other subjects. Sign your commits (git commit -S) — signing is required by policy and checked in review, not enforced by any CI workflow. Every new file starts with an SPDX header following the REUSE Specification (SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 INDUSTRIA DE DISEÑO TEXTIL S.A. (INDITEX S.A.) and SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0). CI runs the REUSE check on every pull request, alongside Repolinter and the Conventional Commits check above.

records.title: Guides
records.content: These guides show how to accomplish specific tasks with Nebula. Pick the group that matches your role, then the guide that states your goal. For what each operating mode does today, side by side, see Operating modes.

records.title: Guides
records.content: Make a requestOpen a session and phrase a request the filter accepts.Generate infrastructureTurn a request into validated Terraform code, reviewed as a plan and report before you apply it.Follow a sessionTrack progress and read the plan, code, and report.Merge and applyHandle a session lock, then open, merge, and apply the pull request.Remediate driftDetect and reconcile drift for a set of resources or a whole Terraform root.Import infrastructureWhat the Import Infrastructure mode does today, and what it does not yet do.

records.title: Guides
records.content: Enable authenticationConnect an OIDC identity provider and grant the first administrator access.Administer users and locksReview any user’s sessions, and manage session locks and roles from the admin panel.Monitor with PhoenixRead Nebula’s traces in Arize Phoenix, and know what a trace contains and omits.Customize promptsManage the prompt registry that encodes your conventions and compliance rules.Configure state backendsChoose who owns Terraform and OpenTofu state: the repository, Nebula, or the deployment.Deploy to productionPlan a production deployment, then work through secrets and credentials, networking and TLS, hardening, and operations.

records.title: Guides
records.content: DevelopmentRun the stack for development, test, type-check, lint, and regenerate the sidecar clients.

records.title: Architecture
records.content: This page introduces Nebula’s runtime components and how they fit together. The rest of this section goes deeper: the end-to-end request flow, the data and state each component owns, and the deployment topology.

records.title: Architecture
records.content: Pan, zoom, search, trace a relationship, switch themes. Open in a new tab /* Progressive enhancement for the block above. Guarded so that a page holding several diagrams runs this once, and deferred to DOMContentLoaded because a parse-time script cannot yet see the diagrams below it. */ (function () { if (window.__archifyEmbed) return window.__archifyEmbed = true /* The viewer's own interactive chrome. Its toolbar and zoom bar are position:fixed, so they always reach the bottom of whatever viewport the iframe gives them -- measuring them would make the height measurement below a fixpoint that can never shrink. Same selector list as docs/diagrams/capture-png.mjs, which hides them instead; here they stay visible and are only excluded from the measurement. */ var CHROME = '.toolbar, .diagram-nav, .focus-chip, .guided-views, .archify-toast, .no-print' var style = document.createElement('style') style.textContent = [ '.archify-actions{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:.35rem .9rem;align-items:baseline;', 'margin-block:-.65rem 1.5rem;font-size:.875rem;line-height:1.5}', '.archify-hint{opacity:.72}', '.archify-frame{width:100%;border:0;display:block}', /* A viewer is ~800KB and takes real time to arrive, so it loads out of the way while the still stays on screen, and is only swapped in once it has something to show. Off-screen rather than display:none: a display:none iframe has no viewport, so the application inside would not lay out, and revealing it would show an empty frame anyway -- which is the whole failure this avoids. */ '.archify-frame[data-archify-loading]{position:absolute;left:-99999px;top:0}', /* Only while the viewer is live. The still image is centred by the theme inside the narrower .imageblock; the frame is centred by this margin inside the wider one. */ '.imageblock.archify-live{margin-inline:auto}', /* The theme insets an image block's contents by 40px, which puts the diagram 40px right of every heading and paragraph on the page. Those do line up with each other: a heading's box starts 64px further left than its text, because the theme carves that gutter with a negative margin and an equal padding to hold the hover anchor. So the column edge is where the text sits, and the diagram was the one thing off it. Dropped on both forms, so activating a block does not shift it. */ '.imageblock.archify-block > .content{padding-inline:0}', ].join('') document.head.appendChild(style) /* The .imageblock wrapper is what escapes the 820px .sectionbody cap (`width: min(calc(var(--content-max-width)*1.25), var(--doc-inset-cap))`), so the viewer is swapped in inside it rather than in place of it. */ function blockFor (actions) { var el = actions.previousElementSibling while (el && !el.classList.contains('imageblock')) el = el.previousElementSibling return el } /* Width is the only lever on how large the viewer draws: its SVG comes out at roughly 0.9x the viewport width it is given, and viewport height barely moves it. But --doc-inset-cap holds .imageblock at 1025px however wide the window gets, which on a large display leaves the whole right half of the article column unused. Track the column instead, so a 2560px screen gets a 1490px frame rather than the still's 945px. */ function columnWidth (block) { var column = block.closest('.doc') return column ? column.clientWidth : 0 } function widen (block) { var width = columnWidth(block) if (width) block.style.width = width + 'px' } /* Height of the real content, which is not the same as the document height: the viewer is a full-viewport application, so both scrollHeight and body height just echo back the height we set. Measure the lowest visible content edge instead, ignoring the fixed chrome. */ function contentHeight (frame) { var doc = frame.contentDocument if (!doc) return 0 var view = doc.defaultView var root = doc.querySelector('.container') || doc.body var nodes = root.querySelectorAll('*') var bottom = 0 for (var i = 0; i < nodes.length; i++) { var node = nodes[i] var computed = view.getComputedStyle(node) if (computed.display === 'none' || computed.visibility === 'hidden' || computed.opacity === '0') continue if (computed.position === 'fixed' || node.closest(CHROME)) continue var rect = node.getBoundingClientRect() if (!rect.width || !rect.height) continue bottom = Math.max(bottom, rect.bottom) } return bottom ? Math.ceil(bottom + 24) : 0 } /* A wider frame makes the viewer draw a larger diagram, which makes it taller, which is the measurement that sized the frame. Settle it over a few bounded passes instead of assuming one is enough, and stop once the change is not worth another reflow. A measurement of zero means the viewer has not laid itself out yet, not that it never will: each one is a whole application, and end-to-end-flow loads five of them at once over a cold cache. Keep waiting, because giving up here strands the frame at its seeded height for good. */ function fit (frame, pass, waits) { var height = contentHeight(frame) if (!height) { if ((waits || 0) < 60) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, pass, (waits || 0) + 1) }, 250) return } var current = parseInt(frame.style.height, 10) || 0 if (Math.abs(height - current) < 8) return frame.style.height = height + 'px' if ((pass || 0) < 3) setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, (pass || 0) + 1, 0) }, 250) } /* Replaces one still with its viewer, then calls `done` to free the slot for the next one -- on load, or on the breaker below, whichever comes first. The still stays on screen for the whole download. An earlier version put the frame in place the moment it was created, which left a blank grey panel where the diagram had been until ~800KB arrived: on a fast static server that is a flicker, on anything slower it is the whole reading experience. So the frame loads off-screen, at the size it is about to occupy, and the swap happens in one synchronous block. */ function activate (actions, done) { var block = blockFor(actions) if (!block || block.classList.contains('archify-live')) return done() var content = block.firstElementChild || block var still = content.querySelector('img') var frame = document.createElement('iframe') frame.className = 'archify-frame' frame.title = actions.dataset.archifyTitle || 'Interactive diagram' /* Load it at the size it will be revealed at, so the viewer lays out for the real column and appearing costs no second reflow. Antora writes no width/height on the still, so one that has not decoded yet measures zero: fall back to a nominal height rather than a collapsed frame. */ var seed = still ? Math.round(still.getBoundingClientRect().height) : 0 frame.style.height = (seed > 120 ? seed : 620) + 'px' frame.style.width = (columnWidth(block) || block.clientWidth || 900) + 'px' frame.setAttribute('data-archify-loading', '') /* Everything that makes the frame visible, in one go, so no intermediate state is ever painted. The frame is never moved in the DOM -- re-inserting an iframe reloads it, which would throw away the wait -- so the still is removed around it instead. */ function reveal () { frame.removeAttribute('data-archify-loading') frame.style.width = '' /* .imageblock is display:flex and .content is a shrink-wrapping flex item: the image sized it by its own intrinsic width, but an iframe has none, so .content would collapse to the UA's 300px iframe default and the frame's width:100% would resolve against an indefinite container. Pin .content to the flex container's width so the percentage has something definite to resolve against. */ content.style.width = '100%' block.classList.add('archify-live') widen(block) for (var i = content.children.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) { if (content.children[i] !== frame) content.children[i].remove() } } /* One viewer loads at a time, so a frame that never fires load would hold the queue for good and strand every diagram below it as a still. Release the slot after a generous wait; this frame still reveals itself if it turns up late. */ var settled = false function settle () { if (settled) return settled = true done() } setTimeout(settle, 15000) frame.addEventListener('load', function () { /* The viewer repeats its own title as an <h1> above the diagram, and every page that embeds one already carries that line as the section heading right above the frame. Two of the same sentence is one too many, and at column width the repeat wraps onto a second line and runs into the viewer's own toolbar. Hidden here rather than removed from the specification: a title is required there, and the "Open in a new tab" page has no surrounding heading to make it redundant. Same document, same origin, so this is a stylesheet and not a message. */ var inner = frame.contentDocument if (inner) { var hide = inner.createElement('style') hide.textContent = '.container > .header{display:none}' inner.head.appendChild(hide) } /* `load` means the viewer's assets arrived and its scripts ran, not that it has drawn: the SVG appears in a later layout pass. Revealing on load alone shows the viewer's own empty panel for a frame or two, so wait for the drawing to exist -- briefly, and then reveal anyway, because a viewer that never draws must not keep the still forever. */ var tries = 0 ;(function ready () { var drawn = false try { drawn = !!(inner && inner.querySelector('svg')) } catch (e) { drawn = true } if (!drawn && ++tries <= 20) return void setTimeout(ready, 100) reveal() settle() /* Only now is the frame in the flow at its final width, so this is where the height measurement belongs. */ setTimeout(function () { fit(frame, 0) }, 400) var width = 0 new ResizeObserver(function () { /* Width only: observing our own height would loop against fit(). */ var next = Math.round(frame.getBoundingClientRect().width) if (next === width) return width = next fit(frame, 0) }).observe(frame) })() }) content.appendChild(frame) frame.src = actions.dataset.archifySrc } /* A page can hold five of these and each is a whole application of roughly 800KB, so they are loaded strictly one at a time. Serial, not merely staggered. An earlier version started one every 900ms, which on a slow origin simply put all five in flight together: a browser opens about six connections per origin, five long downloads take nearly all of them, and the next click on the navigation sidebar gets no socket at all. That is not a slow page, it is a page that has stopped answering -- the network panel shows the navigation cancelled with zero bytes transferred. One viewer at a time bounds the cost to a single connection however slow the origin is, and the reader keeps a still until its replacement is ready, so nothing is lost by waiting. Proximity decides the order and never whether. Two earlier versions let it decide whether, and both stranded the lower diagrams as stills for good: the reader saw a tiny illegible image where a viewer should be. The cause outlives either mechanism. Antora writes no width or height on a still, so every image reflows everything below it as it decodes -- which means a block can be carried into range with no event to announce it. An IntersectionObserver's one-shot entry arrives against a position the block no longer holds; a rect read on scroll is never stale, but nothing reads it once the reader stops scrolling. Working through the whole queue removes that class of failure instead of widening the window it hides in: being near a diagram only brings it forward. */ function enhance () { var pending = [] var actions = document.querySelectorAll('.archify-actions[data-archify-src]') for (var i = 0; i < actions.length; i++) { var block = blockFor(actions[i]) if (!block) continue /* Marks the blocks this script owns, so the stylesheet above can reach them while they are still stills. */ block.classList.add('archify-block') pending.push(actions[i]) } if (!pending.length) return var queued = false var running = false function stop () { window.removeEventListener('scroll', schedule) window.removeEventListener('resize', schedule) } /* Leaving the page ends the queue. Without this, a click on the navigation sidebar races a pump that is about to start another ~800KB viewer: the browser asks for the next document while this page opens one more connection for a viewer nobody will ever see, and on a slow origin the navigation is what waits. The reader reads that as a page that has stopped answering. Nothing below needs the queue once the document is on its way out. */ window.addEventListener('pagehide', function () { pending.length = 0 stop() }) /* One observer for the whole column, not one per diagram. Every live block tracks the same element, so five separate observers on it did the same work five times over on every resize. */ var column = document.querySelector('.doc') if (column) { new ResizeObserver(function () { var live = document.querySelectorAll('.imageblock.archify-live') for (var i = 0; i < live.length; i++) widen(live[i]) }).observe(column) } /* The one place a viewer is ever started. Nothing else calls activate, so there is exactly one download in flight no matter what triggers a pump -- scroll, resize, or the previous one finishing. */ function pump () { if (running || !pending.length) return running = true activate(pending.shift(), function () { running = false if (pending.length) setTimeout(pump, 250) else stop() }) } /* Reorders what is left so anything the reader can nearly see goes next, and never activates anything itself. A diagram already passed keeps its place in the queue: the saving worth having is not loading five viewers at once, not reclaiming one that has scrolled off the top. */ function promote () { queued = false var visible = [] var rest = [] for (var i = 0; i < pending.length; i++) { var block = blockFor(pending[i]) var close = block && block.getBoundingClientRect().top <= window.innerHeight + 400 ;(close ? visible : rest).push(pending[i]) } pending = visible.concat(rest) pump() } function schedule () { if (queued) return queued = true requestAnimationFrame(promote) } window.addEventListener('scroll', schedule, { passive: true }) window.addEventListener('resize', schedule) promote() } if (document.readyState === 'loading') document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', enhance) else enhance() })() Dashed edges are wiring that exists but is not exercised by the checked-in config.yaml: the identity provider is contacted only once oidc.issuer_url is set. The diagram condenses some detail. The four sidecars share one node (authz :8083, mapping :8081, iac :8082, notifications :8080); the core appears as its API layer plus a single "application and adapters" node covering the other three layers; and Redis, the workspaces volume, phoenix-db and the notification and storage backends are carried in the notes beside it rather than drawn. Phoenix is reachable through the proxy at /monitoring/, artifacts land in the nebula-artifacts bucket, and the shipped configuration routes model calls through LiteLLM.

records.title: Architecture
records.content: Component Responsibility Main relationships React SPA (client/web) Session wizard, planning and results views, user page and admin panel. An OIDC public client: it calls /api with a bearer token and streams progress over Server-Sent Events. Built into the Nginx image; reaches the API through Nginx, and the identity provider directly for login Nginx (proxy) Sole public entry point, on ports 80 and 9000: serves the built SPA and proxies /api, the events stream, /monitoring/ and object storage. Browser → core, Phoenix, object storage Core API layer (core/src/api/v1) Routes every request: IaC operations, the progress stream, session reads, repository and pull-request actions, identity and roles, the admin panel, and passthroughs to the mapping and notifications sidecars. One authentication dependency guards all of them but the public OIDC configuration. Delegates to application handlers Application layer (core/src/application) The generate, drift and apply handlers, and the services they orchestrate — filtering, reporting, pull requests, session orchestration. A factory builds a fresh object graph per run. Composes domain services Domain layer (core/src/domains) Entities, value objects and ports, and the services holding the behaviour: the agent loop, session and user management, validation, targeting, the compliance audit, artifact storage, persistence and tracing. Depends only on interfaces Infrastructure layer (core/src/infrastructure) Adapters behind those ports: OIDC, the LiteLLM router, git and workspaces, the iac-sidecar driver, Jinja layouts, object storage, PostgreSQL, Redis and OpenTelemetry. The generated sidecar clients are not part of this layer — they live in core/src/clients, a sibling package. Implements domain ports authz service Cloud project access checks, disabled by default. Disabled, the core answers "authorized" without calling it; enabled, an unreachable sidecar is an error, never an allow. Its user and role endpoints are unused — Nebula keeps those in core-db. Called from the authorize route with the caller’s identity; container-local JSON role store iac service Runs one IaC engine command per asynchronous job — init, validate, plan, show, apply — returning a job id to poll. OpenTofu by default, selected with IAC_BINARY. A reference implementation; production deployments are expected to supply their own. Shares the workspaces volume with the core mapping service Resolves a business identifier to a repository URL, plus a best-effort terraform provider and cloud scope (null means unknown, ask the user); the reference implementation is an identity passthrough. Called through a core passthrough route notifications service Channel-agnostic notify contract; the reference implementation posts colour-coded Slack webhook messages. Fire-and-forget from the core on compliance, apply and pipeline failures; request/response for the support requests the header’s chat bubble sends OpenAPI contracts (contracts/openapi) Source of truth for the four sidecar APIs, with Schemathesis conformance suites. Contracts → generated clients → sidecars core-db (PostgreSQL 17) System of record: twelve tables covering users, sessions, workspaces, rounds, plans, pull requests, reports and artifacts. Core, over asyncpg Redis 8 Fail-open cache for session facts, the last status and finished-session aggregates. No pub/sub, no locks. Core only object-storage (RustFS, Apache-2.0) Default, bundled artifact store (nebula-artifacts): reports, plans, drift JSON and code changes, served to the browser by presigned URL. storage.provider switches to AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage or any other S3-compatible endpoint. Engine state lives in the separate storage.terraform_state_bucket — on by default as shipped. Core through the SDK, browser through Nginx :9000, and the iac sidecar for state workspaces volume Per-run git clones under /workspaces/<session>/<call>. A failed run’s directory is removed; a successful generate round renames its directory to /workspaces/<session>/pinned, which survives until apply discards it or the next generate round replaces it. Mounted by core and iac Phoenix + phoenix-db OpenTelemetry trace collector and UI, and the prompt registry seeded at core boot. Core, over OTLP/HTTP and the Prompts API OIDC identity provider Authenticates users and issues the JWT access tokens the core validates. Any provider with discovery, JWKS and JWT access tokens works; Entra ID, Keycloak, Auth0 and Okta are documented. Browser for login, core for discovery and JWKS; configured under oidc LLM providers Model inference behind the LiteLLM router, in a main and a small role. Selected by llm.model and llm.small_model; credentials in the core’s environment file Git hosting Clone and push over the git CLI; pull requests through the GitHub, Azure DevOps or GitLab REST APIs. Public SaaS hosts only — github.com, gitlab.com without subgroups, dev.azure.com — over HTTPS. GitHub Enterprise Server and self-managed GitLab are not supported today. Selected by git.provider
